Brocade is a type of fabric — a cloth — that has a pattern built into it during the weaving process, resulting in that pattern being slightly raised above the surface of the fabric. Think of it like a texture you can not only see but also feel with your fingertips: the design presses outward, giving the fabric a three-dimensional quality. It is typically heavy, rich-looking, and considered a luxury fabric.

Imagine a deep red cloth. Now imagine golden flowers blooming across its surface — not flat like a print, but lightly puffed out, almost sculptural. The flowers seem to hover above the background. That is what brocade looks like. The patterns are usually ornate and elaborate: florals, leaves, vines, geometric shapes, birds, or abstract swirling motifs. The fabric often has a glossy, lustrous sheen. When metallic threads (gold or silver) are woven into it, brocade can literally shimmer and catch the light.

The contrast between the raised pattern and the flat background is what makes brocade instantly recognizable. It has a visual richness that is hard to mistake for any other fabric.

This is the key to understanding brocade properly.

In most ordinary fabrics, two sets of threads are interlaced — one running horizontally and one vertically — to form the cloth. Simple, flat, uniform.

Brocade goes further. During weaving, extra threads are introduced specifically to create the pattern. These extra threads are woven in only where the design needs to appear, and they loop over multiple base threads at once rather than going under and over every single one. This "floating" technique is what causes those threads to bunch up slightly and sit above the surface, forming the raised pattern.

Crucially, this pattern is not added afterward — it is not painted on, not printed on, and not stitched on top. It is born as the fabric is being made, which is why brocade has such structural integrity and a sense of depth.

Traditionally, brocade was made from silk, which gave it its characteristic luminosity. Silk threads catch light beautifully, so the finished fabric glows. Gold and silver metallic threads were often woven in alongside silk to add further opulence — this variety is sometimes called cloth of gold or cloth of silver, and it was historically reserved for royalty and high nobility.

Today, brocade can be made from synthetic fibres (like polyester or rayon), which makes it more affordable while retaining much of the same visual richness. High-end brocade, however, still uses silk or silk blended with metallic threads.

Because of its weight, texture, and luxurious appearance, brocade has historically been used for things that need to make a statement:

Clothing: Royal robes, ceremonial garments, court dress, wedding gowns, evening jackets, waistcoats, and formal attire of all kinds. A brocade jacket signals occasion and grandeur.

Home furnishings: Curtains, drapes, cushion covers, upholstery on chairs and sofas, bed coverings, and wall hangings. In grand homes and palaces, brocade on the walls or furniture announced wealth.

Religious and ceremonial objects: Vestments worn by clergy, altar cloths, and coverings for sacred objects have long been made in brocade because of its association with dignity and splendour.

Today, brocade appears in high fashion and formal wear, as well as in interior design for spaces meant to feel luxurious.
How Brocade Differs From Similar Things

Since brocade is often confused with other patterned textiles, these comparisons will sharpen your understanding.

Brocade vs. Embroidery: Embroidery is when a pattern is stitched onto an already-finished piece of fabric using needle and thread — the pattern is an addition. Brocade's pattern is woven into the fabric as it is being made — the pattern is inseparable from the cloth itself. One is decoration applied later; the other is decoration built in from the start.

Brocade vs. Damask: Damask is another woven, patterned fabric, but its patterns are created differently — by switching between shiny and matte weave structures using the same thread. The pattern appears because of the contrast in light reflection, not because of raised threads. Damask is also reversible (you see the pattern on both sides, just inverted). Brocade, by contrast, uses extra threads to create visible, tactile relief, and it is not reversible — the back of brocade fabric often looks messy, with floating threads visible, because that is where the pattern threads are travelling between appearances on the front.

Brocade vs. Tapestry: Tapestry is also a woven fabric with imagery, but in tapestry, the woven pattern typically covers the entire surface — there is no distinct background fabric; the design is the fabric. In brocade, there is always a clear background cloth, and the pattern sits upon it.
The Sense of Brocade in a Nutshell

If you had to carry one idea about brocade in your mind, let it be this: brocade is a heavy, ornate, patterned fabric whose designs are woven directly into the cloth, giving them a raised, three-dimensional quality. It is a fabric associated with wealth, ceremony, and visual grandeur — something made not just to cover, but to impress.

When you see a king's robe in a painting, or a bride's elaborate gown rippling with golden flowers, or thick, gleaming curtains in a palace — there is a very good chance you are looking at brocade.
